newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain mourns slain politician, outcry hits ETA.
newsitem.headline: Spain mourns slain politician, outcry hits ETA.

text.p: Spain came to a virtual standstill on Monday as the nation paid its last respects to a young politician kidnapped and brutally killed by Basque separatist guerrillas.

Miguel Angel Blanco, 29, whose death has unified Spaniards in outrage against the guerrilla group ETA, was buried in his hometown in the heart of the northern Basque country in a sombre ceremony broadcast live on state television.
Millions took part in a farewell salute to Blanco, stopping work at noon to observe 10 minutes' silence.

The public outcry found reasonance among elements of the violent separatist movement itself. One town councillor of ETA's political arm, Herri Batasuna, quit and six ETA prisoners joined the 10-minute tribute.
Huge crowds stood motionless on sidewalks in central Madrid. Traffic came to a halt. Flights out of the international airport stopped. Even the stock exchange suspended trading.

In Ermua, where Blanco was a popular town councillor, tens of thousands lined the streets outside the packed chapel where Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Crown Prince Felipe comforted grieving family members.

Crowds, held back by red-jacketed Basque police, chanted "Miguel, Miguel, Miguel" and "Murderers! Murderers!" as his casket was carried through narrow streets en route to its entombment at the town cemetery.

Blanco's killing has sparked a public outcry against ETA, which has assassinated some 800 people in its 29-year struggle for an independent Basque homeland. Demonstrators have taken to the streets in unprecedented numbers to vent their anger.

Rebels abducted Blanco on Thursday and threatened to execute him unless 500 ETA inmates were moved to prisons in the Basque region by 4 p.m. on Saturday. The government said it would never give in to blackmail, and guerrillas shot him just after the deadline passed.
Blanco was found on Saturday dumped on a mountain roadside outside the Basque city of San Sebastian, his hands tied behind his back and two bullets in his brain. He died 12 hours later.
"With the barbarous assassination of Miguel Angel, terrorism has shown its face cold and filled with cruelty," Bishop Ricardo Blazquez told mourners at Blanco's funeral.
"There is no justification for the murder of an innocent," he said of Blanco, a low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party.
Reflecting the depth of public emotion, Spain's King Juan Carlos planned to make a rare televised address to the nation on Monday night in response to Blanco's killing.

The king makes a regular speech at Christmas, but otherwise refrains from addressing the nation. In 1981, the king made a speech after military officers stormed Parliament and held legislators hostage in an attempted coup.
His son Felipe offered his family's support on Monday to "the Basque public in this calm, civil and peaceful struggle against ETA and its accomplices."
Aznar vowed earlier on Monday to intensify the fight against ETA. "We will put a stop to terrorism," he said.
But he warned his countrymen to brace for "painful days" ahead. "Those who only know how to kill, those who only know how to kidnap, will continue doing it."
In official circles, the latest killing was seen as a sign of ETA's weakness and desperation and there was a fear that if cornered the group would respond with more violence.

About 50 young ETA supporters wearing ski masks struck back at the public condemnation early on Monday in the northern city of Pamplona. They attacked the city hall, throwing rocks and bottles at the doors until police intervened, officials said.

Hundreds of thousands of people turned out in more than a dozen Spanish cities overnight to protest against ETA, with the largest gatherings in Madrid and the Basque cities of Bilbao, Vitoria and San Sebastian.

Pope John Paul and other world leaders condemned the killing. Thousands attending a Barcelona concert with opera stars Luciano Pavarotti, Jose Carreras and Placido Domingo fell silent for a minute in solidarity with the Basque people.

Aznar blasted ETA's political arm, Herri Batasuna, calling them "accomplices" to the murder and asking Spaniards to isolate them. Herri Batasuna hold seats in the Basque and Navarre regional parliaments and the national congress.
ETA attacks have stirred public anger before, but it was the death sentence passed against such an innocent victim that cut to the heart of Spanish society.
"Miguel could have been any one of us. That's why it hurts," said one protester in Bilbao.
